title: DfE Decoded #157: Growing Up in the 2020s
author: Paul Urry
summary: Paul Urry reads the DfE's first wave of the Growing Up in the 2020s study, which surveyed nearly 8,000 twelve and thirteen year olds, and asks what it means for school leaders. He starts with the reassuring findings, that most young people are happy and settled, before turning to the harder numbers: 37 percent do not feel they belong at school, 19 percent are persistently absent, and a quarter meet the study's threshold for a probable mental health disorder. His central argument is that attendance, SEND, disadvantage, mental health and belonging cluster in the same children, so schools should connect information rather than manage it in separate silos. He adds findings on family poverty, unequal participation in enrichment, low physical activity, bullying that staff rarely know about, and online life, and notes that primary leaders should read it too. He closes with questions for leaders instead of an action plan, since the study will become more valuable as later waves arrive.
points: The belonging figure, with 37 percent of 12 and 13 year olds not feeling they belong at school, is singled out as the most important number in the report.
Urry argues that disadvantage clusters, so attendance, SEND, mental health and poverty are different faces of the same lived experience and should not be separate improvement priorities.
He draws a distinction between provision and participation in enrichment, asking who actually takes part rather than who is offered a place.
Only around 31 percent of bullied pupils believed staff knew about it, which he uses to challenge the assumption that good behaviour systems reveal what children experience.
He rejects another action plan and recommends a set of probing questions leaders can use with existing data.
quotes: 37% of young people did not agree that they felt a sense of belonging at school. More than one in three.
Attendance isn’t just attendance. Behaviour isn’t just behaviour. SEND doesn’t sit separately from mental health. Disadvantage doesn’t stop at the classroom door.
A register tells us that a child was absent. It doesn’t necessarily tell us why.
Schools are increasingly supporting children whose needs are real but whose formal assessment or diagnosis hasn’t caught up with them.
But children don’t experience school through our organisational chart. They experience all of it at once.
Not who is offered it. Who actually participates? Those are very different questions.
But among those who had experienced bullying, only around 31% believed school staff were aware of it. That should make us think.
Children don’t arrive at the classroom door as data points They bring everything with them.
